newsitem.title: USA: SEC official takes issue with court's muni ruling.
newsitem.headline: SEC official takes issue with court's muni ruling.

text.p: A top SEC enforcement official on Friday said a federal appeals court missed the boat late last month when it threw out the criminal conviction of former Stifel, Nicolaus & Co. executive Robert Cochran.

Colleen Mahoney, deputy director of enforcement at the Securities and Exchange Commission, said the U.S. Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals incorrectly found on March 27 that Cochran was not required to disclose side fees he made on bond deals for the Oklahoma City Airport Trust and the Sisters of St. Mary Healthcare System in St. Louis.

The three-member appeals panel unanimously reversed a federal jury's conviction of Cochran on eight charges of wire fraud and money laundering concerning payments that he allegedly got from firms that he helped to win contracts designed to reinvest issuers' bond proceeds.

The court said Cochran did not have to disclose the fees because, while he had been asked to help the issuers find a good rate on the investment contracts, he had not been specifically contracted to arrange the deal.
The appeals court also saw no evidence that Cochran had tried to harm the healthcare issuer because his actions did not threaten the tax exempt status of the bonds.
Mahoney said that Cochran's failure to tell the issuers about the side fees on the investment contracts was more than a "half truth. I would say it's a whole lie."
"Cochran made misrepresentations on transactions that we thought were material, so the court's analysis of whether or not there was a duty to disclose was unnecesary," she said.

Mahoney said the court's finding that there was no risk to bondholders was "based on a misperception of tax law. I think they underperceived or underappreciated the extent to which" the Internal Revenue Service could move in a declare the offering taxable, she said.
"To an investor, one of the most important things is whether or not (the deal) is in fact tax exempt," she said.
"As a practical matter you may not be able to point to a lot of deals where the IRS has questioned the tax exempt status of an offering," Mahoney said.

"But if yout were to tell an invstor that there were facts regarding this transaction that comporomised a significant piece of the deal, I think that's something a reasonable investor would find material," she said.
